programs.title: The Ostinato Challenge
programs.introText:
An ostinato is a short, repeating musical pattern — the engine that drives some of the most powerful moments in film music. Jaws. The Dark Knight. Inception. Mission: Impossible. The tension in these scores doesn't come from complex harmony or elaborate melody. It comes from one pattern, repeated with intention.

Over 5 days you will build a complete cue from the ground up — starting with the pattern itself, then adding tension, chromatic harmony, a break, and finally assembling everything into a finished piece of music.

creator.name: Filipe Leitão
creator.bio: Film composer, educator, and Associate Professor at Virginia Commonwealth University.

days.title: The Pattern
days.task:
1. Start with rhythm — tap a pattern before you touch your DAW. Something you could tap on a table and immediately feel as urgent or inevitable
2. Now assign notes to that rhythm. Don't think in scales yet — think in intervals. How far does each note move from the last?
3. Loop it for 30 seconds. Does it feel like an engine? Does it make you want to hear what comes next?
days.insideTheScore:
An ostinato is not just a repeated note. It's a musical engine — something that drives the music forward without needing to go anywhere harmonically.

Start with the rhythm. The rhythmic identity of your ostinato is what the listener will feel first — before they process any harmony or melody. [Jaws](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BePfzCOMRZQ) works because of its rhythm as much as its two notes. The Dark Knight's cello pattern is three notes, but it's the relentless subdivision that creates dread.

Once you have a rhythm that feels solid, add pitch. Keep the intervals small — minor seconds and repeated notes create tension naturally. A minor second (one semitone) between two notes sounds unstable, unresolved. Repeating the same pitch several times before moving creates anticipation. You don't need a scale. Chromatic movement is enough.

**What makes a strong ostinato:**
• A clear rhythmic character — syncopated, straight, or off-beat
• Small intervals — minor seconds, minor thirds, or repeated notes
• A range of no more than a fifth — wide leaps lose the sense of inevitability
• A register that leaves room for everything else — low strings or low piano work best as the foundation

[Bach's Prelude in C](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gVah1cr3pU0) is an arpeggio that never changes — the harmonic movement happens above and around it, but the pattern itself is the engine. The power is not in the complexity. It's in the inevitability.

💡 Don't try to make it interesting yet. Make it solid. The ostinato should feel like it could repeat forever without the listener wanting it to stop.

references.title: Why So Serious?
references.composer: Hans Zimmer & James Newton Howard (The Dark Knight)

days.title: Tension Through Repetition
days.task:
1. Take the ostinato from Day 1
2. Build 30 seconds using only the same pattern — no new notes, no new harmony, no drones
3. Start with the ostinato alone. End somewhere more intense. Everything in between is your craft.
days.insideTheScore:
Repetition itself creates tension. The listener hears the pattern loop once, twice, three times — and starts to feel something is coming. Your job today is to use that expectation as a compositional tool, without adding anything new.

**Velocity and syncopation:**
Velocity is not just about loudness — it's about feel. When every note has the same velocity, the pattern sounds mechanical. When you vary it, the pattern starts to breathe and swing. A note with lower velocity on the downbeat and higher velocity on an off-beat creates syncopation without changing a single pitch. Experiment with velocity curves across the pattern — you'll find the ostinato becomes more interesting, more alive, without any new material.

**Density without new notes:**
Adding a second instrument doesn't mean adding a new line. It can mean:
• A second voice entering with just one note of the ostinato, then dropping out — emphasizing that note above the others
• An instrument that plays only the first two notes of the pattern, then disappears, then returns
• Two instruments trading the same motif in different registers, never quite lining up

These micro-entries create accents, surprise, and a sense of multiple forces at work — all from the same pattern.

**Register and dynamics:**
Moving the ostinato or new entries into higher registers increases tension physiologically. A slow, controlled crescendo across 30 seconds is more powerful than a sudden loud moment.

Listen to how [Dream Is Collapsing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OzLhXesNkCI) from Inception uses a guitar and string ostinato with minimal harmonic movement — the tension comes entirely from density and register, not from new material.

💡 For low strings with the weight and articulation to carry a driving ostinato — percussive attacks, natural accent response, and the kind of body that sits under everything else — [Strike Strings](https://www.filipeleitao.com/strikestrings) and [Forge Low Strings](https://www.filipeleitao.com/forgelowstrings) were built for exactly this. For spiccato articulations, [Helix by Orchestral Tools](https://www.orchestraltools.com/helix) is free and responds naturally to velocity and attack.

days.title: Chromatic Harmony Over a Fixed Ostinato
days.task:
1. Keep your ostinato from Day 1 as a fixed pedal in the low or mid register
2. Write a series of chords above it that move chromatically — include chords that don't belong to the key
3. The ostinato never changes. The harmony above it moves freely. Let the friction between them create the emotion.
days.insideTheScore:
This is one of the most powerful techniques in film scoring. The ostinato creates relentless momentum — it sounds inevitable, unstoppable. The chords above it create surprise, color, and emotional shift without ever breaking the rhythm.

John Williams uses this constantly. In [Jaws](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BePfzCOMRZQ), the two-note ostinato stays fixed while the orchestra builds chromatic dissonance above it. In [Duel of the Fates](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D_2bluVPsb0), a rhythmic pattern in the low strings anchors rapid, non-diatonic chord changes in the brass and choir. The listener feels both things at once — the ground is solid, but the sky is unpredictable.

**Chords as colors, not harmony:**
Forget functional harmony here. Don't think about whether the chord belongs to a key or resolves to something. Think about the friction it creates against the ostinato.

If E is a central note in your ostinato — one of its most prominent pitches — then Fm, F#m, and Gm placed above it will create immediate tension. They clash with E. That clash is the point. These chords are not meant to resolve. They are colors — short, accented, staccato or marcato. They land and move on before the ear can settle.

Move chromatically between chords — a half-step up or down. The ear accepts the movement because the ostinato provides continuity below. The ground stays solid. The chords can be as strange as you want.

**Brass accents:**
This is where brass enters. Short, hard accents — sforzando or marcato attacks — land each chromatic chord like a punctuation mark. Place your brass accents on the unexpected chords, not the expected ones. The surprise is the point.

💡 Doubling brass accents with xylophone or snare adds a percussive edge that reinforces the attack without adding weight. Williams uses this constantly — the xylophone gives the accent a sharper, more defined transient that cuts through the texture.

💡 For brass that delivers real weight on short, aggressive accents — the kind of attack that cuts through low strings without sounding thin — [Forge Trumpet](https://www.filipeleitao.com/forgetrumpet) was built for exactly this. Hard attacks, natural decay, cinematic body.

inlineVideos.caption: Duel of the Fates - John Williams (Star Wars: The Phantom Menace)

days.title: Breaking the Pattern
days.task:
1. Write 30 seconds with your ostinato running
2. Break it — but maintain the tension. The break is not a rest. It's a shift.
3. Return to the ostinato quickly — same pattern, or adapted: different tempo, different time signature, or a variation of the original
days.insideTheScore:
Knowing when to break the ostinato is as important as knowing how to build it. But the break is not silence — it's a momentary shift in texture that keeps the listener on edge before pulling them back in.

This is the language of action and suspense scoring. Dense ostinato block — short break — ostinato returns, harder or changed. Repeat. The blocks create momentum. The breaks create anticipation. Together they build unbearable tension.

**What happens during the break:**
The ostinato stops, but the tension doesn't. Under the break, keep a sustained dissonant texture — strings held on a cluster, a low pad, a breath of brass. Something that says: it's not over. The rhythmic pulse can continue underneath, faintly — lighter instruments, a quiet subdivision, just enough to keep the engine running at low power.

The break must be short. Two to four bars at most. Long enough for the listener to feel the absence, short enough that they never fully relax.

**Returning differently:**
The ostinato that returns doesn't have to be identical. Try:
• The same pattern at a faster tempo — more urgency
• A different time signature — 5/4 or 7/8 instead of 4/4 creates immediate disorientation
• A variation of the original motif — same rhythmic identity, different notes

Each return feels like an escalation.

**Percussion at the break:**
A single tímpano hit, a bass drum accent, or a cymbal swell just before the cut marks the transition without announcing it. The percussion makes the break feel inevitable in retrospect.

[No Time for Caution](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpK4cDk2bRs) from Interstellar is a masterclass in this — the organ ostinato builds relentlessly, breaks, and returns with even more weight. [Docking Procedure Test](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7VoulMvA-kY) from For All Mankind uses a marimba-like ostinato with swells and drones that create exactly this kind of sustained tension through breaks.

💡 These short suspense breaks are practically a genre of their own in action scoring. Williams, Zimmer, and Powell all use this structure — dense ostinato block, brief dissonant pause, return harder than before. Listen for it and you'll hear it everywhere.

references.title: Enter Paris
references.composer: Max Aruj & Alfie Godfrey (Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning)

days.title: Full Cue
days.task:
1. Write a complete 60-second cue using everything from this week
2. It must have: a clear ostinato, a build through density and velocity, at least one chromatic harmonic movement, and one intentional break with a return
3. The cue should feel like it belongs in a film
days.insideTheScore:
You have spent four days building the tools. Today you use all of them together.

Before you start, make a plan:

**Structure first:**
Map out your 60 seconds before you write a single note. A simple structure might look like this — ostinato alone for 8 bars, density builds over the next 8, chromatic chords enter, a short break at bar 20, ostinato returns harder, final push to the end. The exact structure is yours. But having a plan prevents you from filling 60 seconds with continuous intensity and wondering why it feels flat.

💡 [CueFlow](https://cueflow.studio) is built exactly for this kind of planning — map your cue structure, emotional arc, and instrumentation before you open your DAW. It turns the plan into a visual scoring map you can follow while you write.

**Layering and synthesis:**
Not everything needs to play all the time. A brass accent that enters only on the chromatic chords is more powerful than brass that plays throughout. A percussion hit that marks the break is more effective than constant percussion.

Synths are not just texture — they're rhythm. A low synth doubling the ostinato with a different articulation, a rhythmic bass synth running underneath the strings, a staccato synth line that reinforces the accents — these add a hybrid score energy that sits between the acoustic and the electronic. The ostinato becomes denser without adding new pitches.

[Assassin Fight](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kZFtqm9t04M) from The Bourne Identity is a perfect example — John Powell builds the cue almost entirely from percussion and synth-based elements, raw and physical, with the ostinato as the rhythmic spine. No orchestral writing. Pure kinetic energy.

💡 For evolving synth textures and hybrid rhythmic elements that already have movement and tension built in — [Eclipse](https://www.filipeleitao.com/eclipse) gives you the raw material. The energy is already there. Your job is to shape it around the ostinato.

**The break and return:**
Plan exactly where the break falls. It should feel inevitable — the listener shouldn't see it coming, but when it arrives it should feel right. The return after the break is your climax. Make it count.

💡 Write the ostinato first. Then build the cue around it. The pattern should feel like it was always there — everything else serves it.

programs.title: Temp Track Challenge
programs.subtitle: Vol. 1
programs.introText:
A temp track is a temporary piece of music that directors use to communicate the emotional direction they want for a scene — before the original score exists.

As a composer, learning to listen to a temp track is a skill. Your job is not to copy it, but to understand why it works emotionally — and then create something original that serves the same feeling.

Each day of this challenge gives you a temp track reference and a specific compositional task. Listen first. Then compose.

creator.name: Filipe Leitão
creator.bio: Film composer, educator, and Associate Professor at Virginia Commonwealth University.

days.title: Epic Melancholy
days.task: Write 60 seconds that capture the feeling of something that will never come back. Don't rush to the climax — let the emotion build slowly, layer by layer.
days.insideTheScore:
Notice how Zimmer builds density gradually over the same chord progression — electric guitar, piano, strings, brass, each entering one at a time. The orchestration grows full, but the harmony stays simple.

To capture this mood, stay in minor — natural minor for pure melancholy, or Dorian if you want a hint of hope (the IV chord becomes major, which opens up the emotional space).

💡 Try letting your melody emerge from the notes of the chords rather than writing a tune first. This is chord-based writing, not melody-based. Let the texture tell the story.

days.title: Magic and Delicacy
days.task: Write 60 seconds that feel enchanted and full of wonder. Think fantasy and romance — this is Elfman at his most tender.
days.insideTheScore:
Start with celesta as your foundation — it's the signature sound of wonder and magic in film scoring. Build from there: add lush high strings for warmth, harp for shimmer, and let the choir carry the melody.

Stay in a major key, but don't just use the I, IV, and V — the ii, iii, and vi chords are all minor, and moving through them adds emotional depth and longing without leaving the key.

Write a singable melody in the mid-to-higher register — stepwise motion with graceful leaps. Countermelodies in the strings under the choir will add lushness without crowding the texture.

days.title: Building Tension
days.task: Write 60 seconds that build unease without ever resolving it. No melody, no rhythm, no release. Just texture growing denser and more unstable.
days.insideTheScore:
This is not about harmony or melody — it's about texture and production. Start with a single layer of long, sustained strings. Let the notes breathe and move slightly within themselves — small, almost imperceptible movements, like particles inside an atom.

Add layers gradually — more strings, pads, occasional harp. No clear tonal center. Let dissonance appear naturally as the layers stack. Use glissandos sparingly for moments of instability. Small synth points can punctuate the texture without becoming melodic.

Most of the work here happens in your DAW, not on the score — automate volume, filter, and reverb across layers to create a slow, delicate accumulation of tension.

💡 For evolving drones and cinematic textures that already move this way, check out [Eclipse by Filipe Leitão](https://www.filipeleitao.com/eclipse)

days.title: Lightness and Charm
days.task: Write 60 seconds that feel light and playful. No drama, no tension — just charm and a smile.
days.insideTheScore:
Fenton builds personality through rhythm and articulation more than melody. The texture here is intentionally sparse — bassoon staccato and pizzicato strings are the foundation. Light, bouncy, almost comedic. Add harpsichord and flute for color.

Keep a steady, constant rhythm and tempo. The melody exists but it's not singable — it moves chromatically, almost sneaking through the harmony. Let chromaticism give it that slightly quirky, playful character.

Leave room for brief moments of comedic pause — a sudden stop, a held breath, then back into the bounce. Those suspense-release moments are a classic comedy scoring technique.

days.title: Vulnerability
days.task: Write 60 seconds where less is always more. Let the layers breathe — they come and go, thicken and dissolve.
days.insideTheScore:
Start with pads as the foundation — minor mode, atmospheric. The piano enters with sparse notes, mostly thirds, simple and unhurried. Solo cello carries the organic warmth, floating above the texture.

Keep the harmony minimal — just two chords. The tension comes from the texture, not the harmony. Add synth particles for movement — subtle, detuned moments of brief dissonance inside the layers, almost imperceptible. A hybrid rhythmic element gives the music a quiet pulse without becoming a beat.

The layers come and go. Let the texture thicken naturally, then pull back. The organic feel lives in the piano and cello — everything else is atmosphere.

Arnalds uses very few notes. Resist the urge to fill the space — the silence is part of the composition. Stay in a minor key but avoid drama. This is not sad — it's vulnerable. There's a difference. Keep the dynamic low throughout. Nothing should feel forced or over-composed.

days.title: Urgency and Action
days.task: Write 60 seconds of music that never stops. Create constant movement — no breathing room, no resolution.
days.insideTheScore:
Powell builds urgency through rhythm and orchestration, not melody. Start with a big drum pattern — toms, metals, nothing classical or orchestral. Raw and physical from the first beat.

Add hybrid synths with a rhythmic, percussive character. Syncopation and unexpected accents shift the downbeat constantly. This creates a sense of disorientation and danger without the listener knowing exactly why.

Harmony is almost nonexistent — just a pedal tone alternating between a few notes. No clear chords. The rhythmic texture is the music.

Build in blocks of contrast — a technique typical of action scoring. A dense section, then a sudden drop, then back in harder. Keep a constant pulse underneath everything.

Avoid anything lyrical — this is pure kinetic energy.

💡 The drum sounds in this cue are not orchestral — they are raw, physical, and heavily processed. If you want that kind of percussion in your own work, [Strike Drums](https://www.filipeleitao.com/strikedrums) was built exactly for this. Hybrid drums designed for film and media composers.

days.title: Reflective and Grand
days.task: Write 60 seconds that feel reflective and still — with moments of contained grandeur that emerge naturally from the texture.
days.insideTheScore:
Start with piano — gentle, unhurried. Let the chords breathe, moving slowly, not on every beat. The emotion lives in the voicing, not in a pre-composed melody. Let the harmony speak for itself.

High strings enter as a pedal — sustained, warm, supporting without moving. As the texture grows, add a female vocal, almost improvised, no lyrics, purely cinematic. Then motion elements that suggest harp — a sense of light and forward movement.

Stay in a clear major tonality. This music is resolved and open — not searching, not dramatic. The grandeur appears briefly, then recedes back into stillness.

programs.title: String Writing Challenge
programs.introText: Over 5 days you will write the same 4-bar chord progression — Am – F – C – G — adding one new layer of craft each day. By Day 5 you will have a complete string cue built from the ground up, one principle at a time.

days.title: Roles & Register
days.task:
1. Write 4 bars using **Am – F – C – G**
2. Assign one role to each section. No overlapping, no doubling yet
3. Use only long notes. Focus on who plays what and where
days.insideTheScore:
A professional string sound comes from how musical information is distributed across the family, not from the library itself.

**Violin I** sits high. Bright, agile, the melodic carrier. The most common mistake is using it as a constant harmonic pad in the mid register. Let it lead.

**Violin II** sits mid-high. Its job is inner harmony and subtle motion. Avoid doubling Violin I in unison. Doubling an octave below or a sixth below are common and effective choices.

**Viola** sits in the middle. Warm, dark, the glue between upper and lower strings. Write it too low and it loses clarity.

**Cello** sits low to mid. Deep, expressive, flexible. Its job here is the bass line. Resist locking it only to root position notes. Give it shape.

**Contrabass** sits below the Cello, always. Foundation and weight. Avoid too much motion or mid-range writing.

💡 If you don't have a string library yet, **[Spitfire LABS](https://labs.spitfireaudio.com)** and **[Berlin Free Orchestra](https://www.orchestraltools.com/berlin-free-orchestra)** are free and include the main articulations.

days.title: Voice Leading
days.task:
1. Return to what you wrote on Day 1
2. Look at how each voice moves from chord to chord
3. Where can a voice stay on the same note instead of jumping? Where can it move by step instead of leaping?
4. Revise each voice with smooth, intentional motion
days.insideTheScore:
Good voice leading is what separates a professional string arrangement from an amateur one.

**Common tones.** When two adjacent chords share a note, keep that voice on the same pitch. In Am – F, for example, the note C is common to both chords. Let it stay.

**Stepwise motion.** When a voice must move, prefer motion by step over leaps. Leaps are fine, but use them intentionally. They draw attention.

**Open spacing in the low register.** Strings sound best with open intervals, especially below the staff. Avoid close harmony between Cello and Viola in a low register. The lower you go, the wider the intervals should be.

Think of the upper strings as free to be closer together, and the lower strings as needing space to breathe.

days.title: Articulation
days.task:
1. Take what you wrote on Days 1 and 2
2. Write the same 4 bars twice — first in legato, then with a different articulation of your choice
3. Listen to how the emotional character changes without a single note being different
days.insideTheScore:
Articulation is one of the most powerful tools in string writing, and one of the most ignored in sample library work.

**Legato.** Smooth, connected phrases. The default emotional language of strings — warmth, continuity, singing quality.

**Staccato.** Short, separated notes. Useful for rhythmic passages and lighter textures.

**Spiccato.** Off-the-string staccato — the bow bounces with each note. More energetic and playful. Common in faster, lighter passages.

**Pizzicato.** The string is plucked, not bowed. Intimate, delicate, percussive depending on context.

**Sul tasto.** Bowing over the fingerboard produces a softer, flute-like sound with less body. Useful for ethereal, distant textures.

**Sul ponticello.** Bowing near the bridge creates a glassy, dissonant, slightly unsettling sound. Very effective for tension and unease.

💡 You can combine multiple articulations within the same passage. For example: Violin I in legato carrying the melody while Cello and Viola provide an arpeggiated accompaniment in pizzicato. The same chord progression can feel like a lullaby or a threat depending entirely on articulation.

days.title: Shape & Dynamics
days.task:
1. Return to your Day 2 version — voice leading, no articulation yet
2. Draw CC1 (Modulation) automation curves for every long note in your piano roll
3. No note should stay at the same volume from start to finish
4. Choose where each note swells, where it retreats, and how each voice breathes
days.insideTheScore:
In a real orchestra, no string player holds a note at a fixed dynamic. Every sustained note has shape — it grows, breathes, tapers. That movement is what makes live strings feel alive.

In a DAW, this is controlled by **CC1 (Modulation)** — drawn as automation in your piano roll or MIDI editor.

**Shape long notes with CC1 automation.** Draw a modulation curve for each sustained note. Even a subtle swell and release transforms a flat sample into something that feels performed. Think of it as adding a breath to each note.

**Use velocity for short articulations.** For staccato, spiccato, and pizzicato, velocity controls the attack intensity. High velocity feels accented and forward. Lower velocity feels softer and receding. Vary it to create a natural rhythmic feel.

💡 Not all voices need to swell at the same time. Try having the Viola swell slightly while Violin I tapers. This creates inner movement and life within the texture, even when the harmony is static.

days.title: Full Texture
days.task:
1. Expand your progression to 60 seconds
2. Apply everything from this week — clear roles, open spacing, smooth voice leading, expressive articulation, and CC1 automation on every long note
3. This is your cue. It should sound like something you would place in a film
days.insideTheScore:
You have been building this cue piece by piece. Today you assemble it.

Before you start, make a plan:

• Who has the melody throughout? Does it stay in Violin I, or does it pass to the Cello for contrast?
• Where does the texture grow and where does it thin out? A professional cue breathes.
• What articulation defines the character of this cue?
• Where are the moments of inner motion — a Viola countermelody, a Cello moving while the upper strings hold?

💡 Write the Cello line first. It anchors everything above it. Once the bass moves with shape and intention, the rest of the section falls into place more naturally.

When you finish, listen back and ask: does every note feel intentional? Is there anything just filling space? Remove it. In string writing, silence and restraint are as powerful as density.

programs.title: No Melody Challenge
programs.introText: The most powerful moments in film music often have no melody at all. Over 3 days you will write a complete cue using only texture, harmony, and density — no singable line, no motif, no theme. Just sound as emotion.

days.title: Texture as Identity
days.task:
1. Write 30 seconds using only sustained layers — strings, pads, or drones
2. No voice should carry a melodic line — no direction, no phrase, no tune
3. Automate volume or filter on at least one layer to create movement within the texture
days.insideTheScore:
Melody implies direction. The moment a sound wants to go somewhere, it becomes a melody. Your job today is to remove that pull entirely — but that doesn't mean static.

A living texture breathes. Use CC1 automation, filter sweeps, or slow volume curves to make layers swell and recede. Let micro-rhythms and subtle dissonances appear inside the sustained sound. Small intervallic tensions between layers — a minor second, a tritone held quietly underneath — create unease without ever suggesting a tune.

**The test:** if you hummed what you wrote, would it sound like a tune? If yes, you have a melody. Remove it. What remains should feel like atmosphere with an inner life.

💡 If you want evolving drones and cinematic textures that already move this way — layers with built-in automation and micro-movement — [Eclipse](https://www.filipeleitao.com/eclipse) was built for exactly this kind of writing.

days.title: Harmony in Motion
days.task:
1. Return to your Day 1 texture
2. Add one harmonic change every 8 bars — move to a related chord, then return or continue
3. The listener should feel tension and release without ever hearing a melody
days.insideTheScore:
Harmony can carry the entire emotional weight of a cue without any melody to guide the ear. The listener feels the change — they just don't know why.

**Slow harmonic rhythm is the key.** A chord change every 8 bars feels like a shift in atmosphere, not a progression. It doesn't suggest melody — it suggests time passing.

**Common tones between chords** keep the texture stable while the harmony moves underneath. In Am – F, the note C is shared. Let it stay. Move only what must move.

days.title: The Full Cue
days.task:
1. Expand your cue to 60 seconds
2. Build to a climax — not through melody, but through density, register, and dynamics
3. The loudest moment should feel inevitable, not sudden
days.insideTheScore:
You have been building without melody for two days. Today you assemble everything into a complete cue.

Before you start, make a plan:

• Where does the texture thin out and where does it fill?
• Which register carries the tension — low drones, high strings, mid pads?
• How does the climax arrive — through accumulation, through a sudden dynamic shift, or through silence before the peak?

The climax of a texture-based cue should feel like pressure finally releasing — not like a melody arriving. The peak is always prepared long in advance.

When you finish, ask: could you hum any part of this? If yes, remove it. That is the challenge.

💡 If you're looking for source material to build this kind of climax — drones and textures that already have inner movement and automation baked in — [Eclipse](https://www.filipeleitao.com/eclipse) gives you the raw material. The density is already there. Your job is to shape it.
